newsitem.title: USA: US transatlantic oil imports hit Latam oil prices.
newsitem.headline: US transatlantic oil imports hit Latam oil prices.

text.p: January U.S. crude imports have a more North Sea and West African flavor due to improved economics for transporting trans-Atlantic barrels, a change that should be even more apparent in February, traders said.
As a result, barrels of South American crude have seen offered prices drop sharply, traders add.

Colombian sweet Cusiana crude was offered before Christmas at a 40 cents premium to U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate(WTI) for delivery at Cushing, Texas, but was recently quoted at a premium of only five cents.
Further, a major crude trader said Brent prices "were becoming more aggressive."
Late Friday Brent was offered into the U.S. Gulf on a delivered basis for February 20-22 at March WTI minus nine cents, and on Monday the discount was about 25 cents for the same time period.

"You never really expect North Sea crudes to be incrementally more economic in the winter time, but the parity gap (taking into account shipping, quality differences etc) with the WTI has closed," said Ken Miller, senior principle for Purvin and Gertz in Houston.
Brent has held a strong premium over the WTI into the fourth quarter of 1996.
"The Brent premium was exceptionally high in September, October and into early November," Miller said.
Expensive Brent prices were driven by the heightened demand from European refiners looking to meet new environmental regulations brought into effect on October 1 for the low sulphur diesel program.
The combination of the switch away from local sour crudes, cold temperatures, North Sea production delays and U.S. heating oil imports propped premiums for Brent.
But by December and into January, the parity between Brent and WTI had narrowed, freeing up more incremental spot overseas barrels for the U.S. Gulf.
As a result, domestic sweet grades have seen differentials to the WTI punctured, and the arbitrage for both Brent and West African crudes widen substantially.

Just Friday, Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James was sold at only a 10 cents premium to the February WTI, down sharply from mid-December when the LLS was sold 60 cts over the marker, and in late November around at a $1.00 edge.
Foreign crude traders said they spotted Norwegian and Brent barrels coming to the U.S. Gulf in the near-term, and said plenty of West African was on offer into February.

"There's a quite a bit of Brent coming in January, around 2 million barrels looks to be on offer (next week). I've also heard Qua Iboe, Bonny Light and Bonny Medium coming into February," said a trader with an oil major.
Still, without an improvement in refinery margins the demand may not be readily apparent for the influx of sweets, Texas trader noted.
On the sour side, parcels of Iraqi and Russian Urals have been confirmed on their way to U.S. destinations.

U.S. refiners Mobil Corp and Clark Refining and Marketing were to take delivery of Iraqi crude in late January and early February from U.S. trader Bayoil, which is bringing over two million-barrels of Basrah Light.
Mobil has since nullified its original contract due to delays in shipping the crude, but was heard re-negotiating terms.
According to U.S. government data, January crude imports were expected to accelerate this year.

The Energy Information Administration forecast first quarter 1997 imports at 7.13 million barrels per day (bpd), second quarter at 7.96 mil bpd, third quarter at 8.16 mil bpd and fourth quarter at 7.78 mil bpd.
Average 1996 imports were seen at 7.4 mil bpd, some 300,000 bpd lower than this year's forecast for 7.7 mil bpd.
In addition to the trans-Atlantic trade, Canadian industry sources expected crude exports to the U.S. between 1.1-1.2 million bpd for January.
-- New York Energy Desk, +1 212 859 1828
